name: Uma Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree, and I maintain warranty software for a tech company. I have enough experience to handle ordinary repairs but ask the claims lead about unusual model codes. Emil repairs cars at a garage; we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and I like making sure a customer is not denied a fair refund because a record was entered badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the warranty app still needs someone to check whether a repaired appliance truly qualifies for a refund. I use an AI helper sometimes on test code, but I check the claim against the repair record before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m an experienced developer with a bachelor’s degree and ordinary pay, and we have about four months of basic bills saved. My husband Emil repairs cars at a garage; we cover the mortgage and two children, though a slow month at the garage makes us cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining warranty rules and ask the claims desk for one disputed repair each week. We’d continue saving 160 monthly if both wages hold and wait another year before replacing the kitchen floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy because a quiet garage month can tighten us already. A modest AI helper does not change the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which claim taught you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fridge repair was logged under the wrong model, so the customer was refused a refund. I found the old serial number with the claims clerk before changing the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI only sometimes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to see a colleague use a tool on a real fault before adding it to my day. If it cannot show the repair record it relied on, I keep the old check.

say: I think **warranty refunds** still need a check against a real repair record.
I use **AI sometimes** on tests, then check the claim myself.
think: I have **four months saved** and ordinary developer pay.
I watch **garage orders** because they help us cover a mortgage and children.
do: **Keep maintaining** warranty rules and review one disputed repair weekly.
**Save 160 monthly** if both wages hold; postpone the kitchen floor.
feel: **Uneasy** about garage income, despite small AI effects.
S0.quote: A modest AI helper does not change the mortgage date.
fieldNote: Her baseline **garage-income variation** keeps the mortgage on her mind even in the mild case.
She needs a **repair record** behind any AI-assisted refund check.

steps.text: Keep maintaining warranty rules and review disputed repairs
Save 160 monthly while both wages continue
Postpone replacing the kitchen floor for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI will take a first pass at claims, code and customer replies, so we need names on final decisions. I would ask our manager which developer hours change before promising a faster service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of my work is checking exceptions that may become automatic. I could lose hours if the company keeps fewer developers, and Emil’s garage pay alone will not meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a colleague to show me an AI test for a wrongly matched appliance model, then practise it on fake claims only if my manager approves paid time. If my hours are cut, I’d ask the claims desk about paid openings and leave only for an offer covering the mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious and alert. I can learn a tool once it proves itself, but I cannot make a reduced pay slip stretch by believing the advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the test works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d give it the fridge claim and five other old model errors. If it cannot trace the serial number, I would not let it approve money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the garage to hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not a mechanic, and I would not pretend my husband’s trade is mine. I know the paperwork side, but I would look for an actual paid claims role first.

say: I want **named final decisions** as AI drafts claims and customer replies.
I want **developer-hour changes** explained before faster service is promised.
think: I expect **exception checks** to become automatic and could lose hours.
I know Emil’s **garage wage** cannot cover our mortgage alone.
do: **Learn AI model checks** on fake claims only if approved on paid time.
**Ask about claims jobs** if hours fall; leave only for bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours despite a possible useful tool.
S1.quote: I cannot make a reduced pay slip stretch by believing the advert.
fieldNote: She will test AI only on **fake claims** with manager-approved paid time, against a known fridge-model error and five other cases.
A **claims-desk move** depends on a real offer covering the household bills.

steps.text: Practise AI appliance-model checks on fake claims only with approved paid time
Ask about paid claims-desk openings if developer hours fall
Accept claims work only if pay covers mortgage and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write our code and decide warranty claims as well as people. Robots that repair cars may come around 2031, so Emil’s hands-on work has a later date than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my software wage could end while the mortgage still needs two pay cheques. Four months saved helps, but I cannot tell our children that it is a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company this month for a written job date and tell Emil we should keep the old kitchen floor. If my developer role ends after AGI arrives in 2028, I’d apply for paid warranty-dispute posts only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; we’d call the lender before arrears if the search runs long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed but able to speak. The hard part is explaining to the children why I am home while their father is still driving to the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say my coding job may have ended, but I am looking for paid work and the house is still our home. I would not promise a start date that no employer has given me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Emil’s garage work carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a short while, perhaps if orders stay up and we cut spending. Robots in 2031 mean even that work could change later, so I would not build a permanent plan on it.

say: I say **thinking AGI by 2028** reaches my code and warranty decisions.
I know **garage robots around 2031** could affect Emil later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end before the mortgage is paid.
I know **four months saved** is time to search, not a new income.
do: **Request a job date** and keep the old kitchen floor.
**Apply for dispute work** only if displaced after 2028 and vacancies cover bills.
**Call the lender** before arrears only if the job search runs long.
feel: **Alarmed** by losing my wage before Emil’s hands-on work changes.
S2.quote: I would not promise a start date that no employer has given me.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 desk work** from robots reaching garage repairs around 2031.
Her **lender call** is a contingency if a long job search risks arrears; no income support is assumed from the bank.

steps.text: Keep the old kitchen floor instead of spending on a replacement
Apply for paid warranty-dispute vacancies if displaced after 2028 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to teach people how to spot a false warranty claim. Robots might reach hands-on garage repairs around 2034, but the software change comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at difficult claims while still earning, though AGI may reason through them too. Emil and I might save more if garage orders remain steady, so I want a plan that does not need a sudden loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the claims lead for two disputed repair files each month with names removed and write my decision before seeing the actual result, if my manager approves paid time. We’d add 120 monthly to emergency savings if both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d seek paid claims-review posts only where vacancies remain and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but more able to practise. I want to know whether I can explain a decision before an AI answer makes it look easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write on each file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d list the repair date, serial number and reason for granting or denying a refund. I would ask the claims lead which piece of evidence I missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no files to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my current code work and ask for old public examples. I would not call reading a sales brochure retraining.

say: I want **false warranty claims** taught before AGI reaches the code in 2031.
I know **garage robots around 2034** may later reach Emil’s work.
think: I might improve at **hard claims**, though AGI could reason through them too.
I could build **more savings** if both wages and garage orders hold.
do: **Study two anonymized claims** monthly only with manager-approved paid time.
**Seek paid claims review** only if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but able** to practise on real evidence.
S3.quote: I want to know whether I can explain a decision before an AI answer makes it look easy.
fieldNote: Her **blind decision practice** is real learning on anonymized files, conditional on paid approval.
Saving still depends on **two wages**, including variable garage orders that could slow before she reaches the larger reserve.

steps.text: Study two anonymized claim files monthly only with manager-approved paid time
Save 120 monthly while both wages continue
Seek paid claims-review vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets families pay down debt and show apprentices how a repair record becomes a fair decision. Robots for garage work may follow around 2039, after software claims change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but the mortgage could still need two wages. I could build a six-month reserve if both jobs last, while accepting that AI may handle both code and claim review by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining warranty rules and build a private notebook of model-matching errors without customer names. We’d pay 150 extra monthly toward the mortgage if both wages hold; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid repair-office roles only if posts exist and the wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the long change, but the next few years feel manageable. I would not make the children pick a career to solve my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me remember which model code matched which repair and why. If I need a job, I can show my warranty-check method without taking a customer’s file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change towns for that role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written offer covering moving costs and a new housing payment. There are some local software firms, so I would ask them first while I still have wages.

say: I want **fair repair decisions** taught before AGI reaches claims software in 2036.
I know **garage robots around 2039** arrive after the code changes.
think: I could build a **six-month reserve** if both jobs continue.
I know **code and claims review** may both be automated by 2036.
do: **Keep maintaining rules** and record model errors without customer names.
**Pay 150 extra** on the mortgage if both wages hold.
**Check** local software firms first; seek bill-covering repair-office posts after 2036 displacement; move only for written relocation- and housing-covering offer.
feel: **Uneasy later**, with the next few years looking manageable.
S4.quote: I can show my warranty-check method without taking a customer’s file.
fieldNote: Her **model-error notebook** is a familiar way to show work without exposing customers.
The **mortgage prepayment** depends on both wages, not a promised AI benefit.
She checks **local software firms** while employed; relocation needs written pay for moving and new housing.

steps.text: Keep maintaining warranty rules and record anonymized model errors
Pay 150 extra monthly toward the mortgage while both wages hold
Check local software firms first; apply to bill-covering repair-office posts if displaced after 2036
Move only for written offer covering moving costs and new housing payment

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my software wage could end before we have paid off the mortgage. A written job date and actual paid claims work that covers our bills would help; I would call the lender early if the search ran long.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a robot will ever explain a repair to a customer. I would want someone at the garage or claims desk to own the answer. A customer deserves a named person at the garage or claims desk who owns a repair decision.

headlineQuote: A customer deserves a named person at the garage or claims desk who owns a repair decision.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and four months saved.
She and Emil cover **two children** and a mortgage, with garage orders affecting his wage.
She uses AI **occasionally after proof**, checking warranty decisions against repair records.
Her **2028 concern** is her software pay; robots could reach Emil’s garage work later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage while the household still pays a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date** and a real paid claims role covering bills would help; she would call the lender if needed.
